title: How does physical distance from the epicenter influence misinformation sharing? The roles of negative affect and social media engagement
screen_reason: Although the paper's aim is a moderated-mediation model of distance-to-epicenter and misinformation sharing, the descriptive statistics report a share of survey respondents who self-reported having shared COVID-19 information online that they later found to be false (21.4% of N = 1094). That is an observed (not hypothetical) self-reported sharing share with an explicit denominator, meeting the RECALL criterion.

estimates.platform: online platforms including WeChat Moments / WeChat groups (self-reported)
estimates.date: Survey fielded from 22 February 2021; the sharing question refers to behaviour during the COVID-19 outbreak (February 2020)
estimates.measure_type: % of survey respondents who reported having shared COVID-19 information online that they later found to be incorrect
estimates.value_raw: 21.4% of respondents; mean score for misinformation sharing 0.21 (SD = 0.41), N = 1094
estimates.denominator: 1,094 valid respondents to an online questionnaire (WJX platform) drawn from 27 Chinese provinces and autonomous regions
estimates.definition: A respondent counted in the numerator if they answered 'Yes' to: 'During the pandemic, have you ever shared information or messages about COVID-19 online (including on WeChat Moments/WeChat groups) that you later found to be incorrect?' (coded 1 = Yes, 0 = No). Falsity is the respondent's own retrospective judgement; no window other than 'during the pandemic'.
estimates.misinfo_def: "Misinformation is defined as 'incorrect or misleading content presented as factual statements' (Green and Donahue, 2018, p. 109). Unlike disinformation, which is deliberately created to deceive, misinformation is characterized by the unintentional dissemination of false information"
estimates.source_quote: The descriptive statistics indicate that the mean score for misinformation sharing was 0.21 (SD= 0.41), with 21.4% of respondents reporting that they had shared COVID-19-related news or information on online platforms (e.g., WeChat Moments/WeChat groups) that was later found to be false.
estimates.page_loc: Results, 'Descriptive statistics and correlation analysis', p. 5; Table 1 (M = 0.21, SD = 0.41, N = 1094)
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Single self-report binary item adapted from Chen et al. (2015); the respondent alone judges whether the shared information was 'later found to be incorrect'. No external verification, no reliability statistic for this item (Cronbach's alpha 0.89 is reported for the negative-affect scale only). Data-quality screens: completion-time thresholds (<5 min or >30 min excluded), IP-address duplicate check, embedded attention checks.
estimates.moderator_quote: The questionnaire was administered through WJX (https://www.wjx.cn), an online survey platform extensively used in China for its efficiency in managing large-scale surveys. ... After removing invalid responses, 1094 valid questionnaires were obtained from 27 provinces and autonomous regions in China, covering areas with varying pandemic severity.
estimates.notes: Data-collection year coded 2021 (survey commenced 22 February 2021); the behaviour asked about is retrospective to the early-2020 outbreak, so the recall window is roughly one year - relevant to recall bias. sampling_frame coded convenience rather than survey_sample: the study describes recruitment across provinces and states the sample 'closely mirror[s] the general profile of Chinese internet users', but no probability frame, quota design or response rate is reported for a self-administered online questionnaire platform. The 21.4% is a share of respondents (a person-level self-report), not a share of shared items.

missed_or_uncertain: (1) 31% of respondents relied on social media as their primary source of pandemic information - a media-use share, not misinformation exposure or sharing, so no row. (2) The '80% of respondents reported frequent social media use during the pandemic' figure in the literature review is cited from Gao et al. (2020), i.e. from elsewhere, and is excluded per R8. (3) All regression output (binary logistic beta = -0.549 for distance; mediation/moderation coefficients in Tables 2-4) are associations, not prevalence shares. (4) No subgroup shares of misinformation sharing by distance band (Wuhan / rest of Hubei / outside Hubei) are reported anywhere, only the correlation r = -0.11, so the headline 21.4% could not be split by proximity. (5) Demographic percentages (45.2% male etc.) describe the sample, not misinformation. (6) The mean 0.21 (SD 0.41) and the 21.4% are the same quantity expressed twice (a binary item), so only one row was created; 21.4% of 1094 implies roughly 234 respondents, but that count is not stated verbatim and was not entered as a count.

rob.design: Cross-sectional online questionnaire (WJX platform), fielded from 22 February 2021 in China; 1,094 valid responses from 27 provinces/autonomous regions after removing invalid submissions. No sampling frame, recruitment source, invitation count or response rate is reported, so non-response cannot be assessed. Quality controls: 3-day soft launch, completion-time thresholds (<5 min / >30 min), IP-based duplicate detection, attention-check items. Misinformation sharing measured with a single retrospective binary self-report item (no reliability statistic); negative affect measured with a validated 6-item Chinese emotion scale (Cronbach's alpha = 0.89). Analysis: binary logistic regression and PROCESS Model 7 with 5,000 bootstrap resamples. Recall period is about 12 months before fielding.
